items.title: Finite orthogonal sums of self-adjoint operators and of bounded operators
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), the choice
hypothesis of the cited definitions of the adjoint. Fix an integer $r\ge1$, let
$H_{1},\dots,H_{r}$ be complex Hilbert spaces with inner products linear in the
first argument ([[def-hilbert-space]]), and let
$$H:=\bigoplus_{l=1}^{r}H_{l},\qquad \bigl\langle (x_{l}),(y_{l})\bigr\rangle:=\sum_{l=1}^{r}\langle x_{l},y_{l}\rangle_{H_{l}},$$
be their orthogonal sum. For each $l$ let $A_{l}:D(A_{l})\subset H_{l}\to H_{l}$
be a densely defined self-adjoint operator
([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]) and put
$$D(A):=\Bigl\{(x_{l})\in H:\ x_{l}\in D(A_{l})\ \text{for all }l,\ \sum_{l=1}^{r}\|A_{l}x_{l}\|_{H_{l}}^{2}<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad A(x_{l}):=(A_{l}x_{l}).$$
Then:

(a) $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, $D(A)$ is a dense linear subspace of $H$,
and $A:D(A)\to H$ is a linear operator;

(b) $A$ is symmetric and self-adjoint, and
$\|Ax\|^{2}=\sum_{l=1}^{r}\|A_{l}x_{l}\|_{H_{l}}^{2}$ for every $x\in D(A)$;

(c) if $B_{l}\in\mathcal B(H_{l})$ for every $l$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), then $B:=\bigoplus_{l=1}^{r}B_{l}$, defined
by $B(x_{l}):=(B_{l}x_{l})$ for all $(x_{l})\in H$, is bounded with
$$\|B\|=\max_{1\le l\le r}\|B_{l}\|$$
([[def-operator-norm]]), its adjoint is
$B^{*}=\bigoplus_{l=1}^{r}B_{l}^{*}$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]), and $B$
is unitary if every $B_{l}$ is unitary.

No assertion is made about infinite orthogonal sums: only the finite case is
proved here.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice; the integer $r\ge1$; complex Hilbert spaces $H_{1},\dots,H_{r}$ with pairings linear in the first argument; densely defined self-adjoint operators $A_{l}$ on $H_{l}$; bounded operators $B_{l}\in\mathcal B(H_{l})$; vectors $x=(x_{l}),y=(y_{l})\in H$; unit vectors $u_{l}\in H_{l}$; scalars $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$.

[F1] **The orthogonal sum.** $\langle(x_{l}),(y_{l})\rangle=\sum_{l}\langle x_{l},y_{l}\rangle_{l}$ is a Hermitian sesquilinear form, linear in the first argument, with $\langle x,x\rangle=\sum_{l}\|x_{l}\|^{2}\ge0$ and equality exactly for $x=0$; the induced norm is $\|x\|^{2}=\sum_{l}\|x_{l}\|^{2}$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A complex Hilbert space is complete for its norm.

[F2] **Adjoints.** For a densely defined operator $T$ on a Hilbert space, $D(T^{*})$ consists of those $y$ for which $x\mapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle$ is a bounded linear functional on $D(T)$, and $T^{*}y$ is its Riesz representative; $T$ is symmetric when $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$, and self-adjoint when $D(T^{*})=D(T)$ and $T^{*}=T$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). In particular a symmetric operator with $D(T^{*})\subseteq D(T)$ is self-adjoint.

[F3] **Bounded operators.** For $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ one has $\|Bx\|\le\|B\|\,\|x\|$, and $\|B\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}\|Bx\|$ is attained as a supremum over the unit ball ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]]). The Hilbert adjoint $B^{*}$ is characterized by $\langle Bx,y\rangle=\langle x,B^{*}y\rangle$ for all $x,y\in H$; $B$ is unitary exactly when $B^{*}B=BB^{*}=I$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; verify the Hilbert-space axioms componentwise, prove density, symmetry and the adjoint computation slot by slot, and compute the norm and adjoint of a bounded orthogonal sum.

**Given:** The data of the statement and [F1]-[F3].

1.1 [Hilbert-space axioms] [F1] gives sesquilinearity, Hermitian symmetry and positive definiteness of the displayed form, since all of these are checked componentwise and the sum over $l=1,\dots,r$ is finite. For completeness let $(x^{(n)})_{n}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $H$, $x^{(n)}=(x^{(n)}_{l})_{l}$. For each $l$ and all $m,n$ one has $\|x^{(n)}_{l}-x^{(m)}_{l}\|_{l}\le \|x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\|$, so $(x^{(n)}_{l})_{n}$ is Cauchy in $H_{l}$ and converges to some $x_{l}\in H_{l}$; then $\sum_{l}\|x_{l}\|^{2}= \lim_{n}\sum_{l}\|x^{(n)}_{l}\|^{2} \le\limsup_{n}\|x^{(n)}\|^{2}<\infty$ because a Cauchy sequence is bounded, so $x:=(x_{l})\in H$, and $\|x^{(n)}-x\|^{2}=\lim_{m}\sum_{l}\|x^{(n)}_{l}-x^{(m)}_{l}\|^{2} =\lim_{m}\|x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\|^{2}$, which tends to $0$ as $n\to\infty$ uniformly in $n$ because the sequence is Cauchy; hence $x^{(n)}\to x$. This proves (a) for the space. [F1, algebra]

1.2 [Density and linearity of the domain] The algebraic sum $\bigoplus_{l}D(A_{l})\subseteq D(A)$: each $(x_{l})$ with $x_{l}\in D(A_{l})$ has a finite sum $\sum_{l}\|A_{l}x_{l}\|^{2}$. It is dense in $H$: given $x\in H$ and $\varepsilon>0$, density of $D(A_{l})$ gives for each $l$ a vector $y_{l}\in D(A_{l})$ with $\|x_{l}-y_{l}\|<\varepsilon/\sqrt r$, so $y:=(y_{l})\in\bigoplus_{l}D(A_{l})$ and $\|x-y\|^{2}=\sum_{l}\|x_{l}-y_{l}\|^{2}<\varepsilon^{2}$. The set $D(A)$ is a linear subspace because $\sum_{l}\|\alpha A_{l}x_{l}+\beta A_{l}y_{l}\|^{2}\le 2|\alpha|^{2}\sum_{l}\|A_{l}x_{l}\|^{2} +2|\beta|^{2}\sum_{l}\|A_{l}y_{l}\|^{2}<\infty$ for $x,y\in D(A)$, and $A$ is linear because each $A_{l}$ is. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 [Symmetry] Let $x,y\in D(A)$. Then $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\sum_{l}\langle A_{l}x_{l},y_{l}\rangle_{l} =\sum_{l}\langle x_{l},A_{l}y_{l}\rangle_{l}=\langle x,Ay\rangle$, because each $A_{l}$ is self-adjoint and hence symmetric; all sums are finite. [F2, algebra]

1.4 [The adjoint domain] Let $y\in D(A^{*})$ and $z:=A^{*}y$. For fixed $l$ and each $u\in D(A_{l})$ let $x^{(l,u)}\in H$ have $u$ in slot $l$ and $0$ in all other slots; then $x^{(l,u)}\in D(A)$ and $Ax^{(l,u)}$ has $A_{l}u$ in slot $l$. Using [F2] for $A$ and the componentwise pairing, $\langle A_{l}u,y_{l}\rangle_{l} =\langle Ax^{(l,u)},y\rangle=\langle x^{(l,u)},z\rangle =\langle u,z_{l}\rangle_{l}$ for every $u\in D(A_{l})$. Hence $u\mapsto\langle A_{l}u,y_{l}\rangle_{l}$ is bounded on $D(A_{l})$, represented by $z_{l}$; so $y_{l}\in D(A_{l}^{*})=D(A_{l})$ and $A_{l}^{*}y_{l}=z_{l}$, that is $A_{l}y_{l}=z_{l}$. Summing, $\sum_{l}\|A_{l}y_{l}\|^{2}=\sum_{l}\|z_{l}\|^{2}=\|z\|^{2}<\infty$, so $y\in D(A)$ and $Ay=z$. Hence $D(A^{*})\subseteq D(A)$ and $A^{*}y=Ay$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 [Self-adjointness] Step 1.3 gives symmetry; symmetry gives $D(A)\subseteq D(A^{*})$ with $A^{*}$ agreeing with $A$ there ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]]), and step 1.4 gives the converse inclusion, so $A^{*}=A$ by [F2]. The norm identity is [F1] applied to $Ax=(A_{l}x_{l})$. This proves (b). [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, F1, F2, algebra]

3.1 [Bounded sums] Let $B_{l}\in\mathcal B(H_{l})$. For $x\in H$, $\|Bx\|^{2}=\sum_{l}\|B_{l}x_{l}\|^{2} \le(\max_{l}\|B_{l}\|)^{2}\sum_{l}\|x_{l}\|^{2} =(\max_{l}\|B_{l}\|)^{2}\|x\|^{2}$, so $B$ is bounded with $\|B\|\le\max_{l}\|B_{l}\|$ by [F3]. Pick $l_{0}$ with $\|B_{l_{0}}\|=\max_{l}\|B_{l}\|$ and, for $\eta>0$, a unit vector $u_{l_{0}}\in H_{l_{0}}$ with $\|B_{l_{0}}u_{l_{0}}\|\ge\|B_{l_{0}}\|-\eta$ [F3]; then the vector with $u_{l_{0}}$ in slot $l_{0}$ and $0$ elsewhere is a unit vector of $H$ with $\|Bx\|=\|B_{l_{0}}u_{l_{0}}\|\ge\|B\|_{\sup}-\eta$, where $\|B\|_{\sup}=\max_{l}\|B_{l}\|$; letting $\eta\to0$ gives $\|B\|\ge\max_{l}\|B_{l}\|$. Hence $\|B\|=\max_{l}\|B_{l}\|$. For $B_{l}^{*}$ the adjoint of $B_{l}$, the operator $\bigoplus_{l}B_{l}^{*}$ satisfies $\langle Bx,y\rangle=\sum_{l}\langle B_{l}x_{l},y_{l}\rangle_{l} =\sum_{l}\langle x_{l},B_{l}^{*}y_{l}\rangle_{l} =\langle x,(\bigoplus_{l}B_{l}^{*})y\rangle$ for all $x,y\in H$, so $B^{*}=\bigoplus_{l}B_{l}^{*}$ by [F3]. If every $B_{l}$ is unitary then $B^{*}B=\bigoplus_{l}B_{l}^{*}B_{l}=\bigoplus_{l}I_{H_{l}}=I$ and likewise $BB^{*}=I$, so $B$ is unitary. This proves (c). [F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- **Where the finiteness is used.** Both the norm identity of (b) and the norm
  formula of (c) are finite-sum statements; for infinite orthogonal sums the
  domain condition in (b) and the supremum in (c) require separate arguments,
  and no such statement is made here.
- **Choice.** Only the Axiom of Countable Choice is declared, as the choice
  hypothesis of the cited definitions of the adjoint; the argument itself
  handles finitely many slots and makes no further selection.

items.title: Unitary identifications of the component-valued wave-function space
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix integers
$d\ge1$ and $r\ge1$, let $H:=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ with the Euclidean
integral pairing ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]), let
$$H^{(r)}:=L^{2}\bigl(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r}\bigr),\qquad \langle f,g\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb R^{d}}\sum_{l=1}^{r}f_{l}(x)\overline{g_{l}(x)}\,dx,$$
and let $\mathbb C^{r}$ carry the standard inner product with orthonormal basis
$e_{1},\dots,e_{r}$ ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]).
Write $H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}$ for the completed tensor product of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] with inclusion $\kappa$.
Then:

(a) the map
$$\Psi_{0}\Bigl((f_{l})\Bigr):=\bigl(x\mapsto(f_{1}(x),\dots,f_{r}(x))\bigr)$$
is a well-defined unitary isomorphism $\bigoplus_{l=1}^{r}H\to H^{(r)}$, and
$$\|\Psi_{0}(f)\|_{H^{(r)}}^{2}=\sum_{l=1}^{r}\|f_{l}\|_{H}^{2},\qquad \langle\Psi_{0}(f),\Psi_{0}(g)\rangle=\sum_{l=1}^{r}\langle f_{l},g_{l}\rangle_{H};$$

(b) the assignment on elementary tensors
$\Theta_{0}(\kappa(u\otimes e_{l})):=\iota_{l}(u)$, where $\iota_{l}(u)$ is
the $r$-tuple with $u$ in slot $l$ and $0$ elsewhere, extends uniquely to a
surjective linear isometry $\Theta:H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}\to H^{(r)}$
(so $\Theta$ is unitary), and
$\Theta(\kappa(u\otimes z))=\sum_{l=1}^{r}z_{l}\,\iota_{l}(u)$ for all
$u\in H$, $z=\sum_{l}z_{l}e_{l}\in\mathbb C^{r}$;

(c) for every $a\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb R^{d})$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^{d}$ one
has the intertwining identities
$$\Theta^{-1}\bigl(a\cdot\Theta(w)\bigr)=(M_{a}\otimes I_{\mathbb C^{r}})w,\qquad \Theta^{-1}\bigl(T_{v}^{(r)}\Theta(w)\bigr)=(T_{v}\otimes I_{\mathbb C^{r}})w\qquad(w\in H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}),$$
where $M_{a}$ is multiplication by $a$, $T_{v}$ is the Euclidean translation
$T_{v}h:=h(\cdot-v)$ of [[lem-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-momentum-operators-self-adjoint]]
clause (c), $T_{v}^{(r)}$ is its componentwise action on $H^{(r)}$, and the
bounded amplifications are those of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice; integers $d,r\ge1$; the spaces $H$, $H^{(r)}$ and the orthonormal basis $e_{1},\dots,e_{r}$ of $\mathbb C^{r}$; the completed tensor product $H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}$ with inclusion $\kappa$; tuples $f=(f_{l}),g=(g_{l})\in\bigoplus_{l}H$; an element $w\in H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}$; $a\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb R^{d})$; $v\in\mathbb R^{d}$.

[F1] **Tensor construction.** $H\odot\mathbb C^{r}$ carries the sesquilinear form $\langle\sum_{i}u_{i}\otimes z_{i},\sum_{j}u_{j}'\otimes z_{j}'\rangle =\sum_{i,j}\langle u_{i},u_{j}'\rangle_{H}\langle z_{i},z_{j}'\rangle_{\mathbb C^{r}}$, which is an inner product; for finite-dimensional subspaces with orthonormal bases, expansions diagonalize it; the completion $H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}$ with inclusion $\kappa$ is a complex Hilbert space with dense image and $\|\kappa(u\otimes z)\|=\|u\|\,\|z\|$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] clauses (a)-(c)). Moreover $(e_{l})_{l}$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb C^{r}$, so the elementary tensors $u\otimes e_{l}$ have $\bigl\langle\sum_{l}u_{l}\otimes e_{l},\sum_{l}u_{l}'\otimes e_{l}\bigr\rangle =\sum_{l}\langle u_{l},u_{l}'\rangle$ and $\bigl\|\sum_{l}u_{l}\otimes e_{l}\bigr\|^{2}=\sum_{l}\|u_{l}\|^{2}$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] clause (b)).

[F2] **Bounded amplifications.** For bounded $S\in\mathcal B(H)$ and $T\in\mathcal B(\mathbb C^{r})$ there is a unique bounded $S\otimes T$ on $H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}$ with $(S\otimes T)\kappa(u\otimes z) =\kappa(Su\otimes Tz)$ and $\|S\otimes T\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$; for $S=M_{a}$ bounded and $T=I$ this is $M_{a}\otimes I$, and for $S=T_{v}$ unitary and $T=I$ it is $T_{v}\otimes I$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] clauses (a),(d)).

[F3] **Euclidean $L^{2}$.** For $f=(f_{1},\dots,f_{r})\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ each component $f_{l}$ is a well-defined class in $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$, two representatives that agree almost everywhere have almost everywhere equal components, and $|f_{l}|\le\|f\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}$ pointwise, so $\|f_{l}\|_{H}\le\|f\|_{H^{(r)}}$; conversely every $r$-tuple of $L^{2}$ classes defines a class in $H^{(r)}$ ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

[F4] **Tonelli and Cauchy-Schwarz.** For $\sigma$-finite measure spaces, integrals of nonnegative product-measurable functions may be iterated ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); for vectors $f,g$ in an inner product space $|\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|\,\|g\|$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]]).

[F5] **Dense extension.** A bounded linear map on a dense subspace of a normed space extends uniquely to a bounded linear map on the whole space, with the same norm ([[thm-extension-of-a-bounded-map-from-a-dense-subspace]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; check well-definedness of the component map, compute norms and pairings by Tonelli and Cauchy-Schwarz, and build the tensor identification isometrically on the algebraic tensor product before extending by density.

**Given:** The data of the statement and [F1]-[F5].

1.1 [Well-definedness of $\Psi_{0}$] Let $(f_{l})\in\bigoplus_{l}H$ and let $(\tilde f_{l})$ be another choice of representatives with $\tilde f_{l}=f_{l}$ almost everywhere for each $l$; then $(\tilde f_{1},\dots,\tilde f_{r})=(f_{1},\dots,f_{r})$ almost everywhere, so $\Psi_{0}(f)$ is the same class of $H^{(r)}$ and $\Psi_{0}$ is well defined [F3]. It is complex-linear because addition and scalar multiplication in $H^{(r)}$ are componentwise. [F3, algebra]

1.2 [Isometry] For $f=(f_{l})$ and $g=(g_{l})$ in $\bigoplus_{l}H$, the functions $x\mapsto\sum_{l}|f_{l}(x)|^{2}$ is nonnegative and measurable, so [F4] gives $\int_{\mathbb R^{d}}\sum_{l}|f_{l}|^{2} =\sum_{l}\int_{\mathbb R^{d}}|f_{l}|^{2}=\sum_{l}\|f_{l}\|_{H}^{2}$, that is $\|\Psi_{0}(f)\|^{2}=\|f\|^{2}_{\oplus}$; the map $\Psi_{0}$ is thus an isometry. For the inner product, Cauchy-Schwarz gives $\int_{\mathbb R^{d}}\sum_{l}|f_{l}||g_{l}| \le\sum_{l}\|f_{l}\|_{H}\|g_{l}\|_{H} \le\bigl(\sum_{l}\|f_{l}\|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} \bigl(\sum_{l}\|g_{l}\|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}<\infty$, so the integrand $\sum_{l}f_{l}\overline{g_{l}}$ is integrable and Tonelli applies to its real and imaginary parts, giving $\langle\Psi_{0}(f),\Psi_{0}(g)\rangle =\int\sum_{l}f_{l}\overline{g_{l}}=\sum_{l}\langle f_{l},g_{l}\rangle_{H}$. [F3, F4, algebra]

1.3 [The tensor identification on the algebraic tensor product] On elementary tensors put $\Theta_{0}(\kappa(u\otimes z)):=\sum_{l}z_{l}\iota_{l}(u)$ for $z=\sum_{l}z_{l}e_{l}$. The map $(u,z)\mapsto\sum_{l}z_{l}\iota_{l}(u)$ $H\times\mathbb C^{r}\to H^{(r)}$ is $\mathbb C$-bilinear, so $\Theta_{0}$ factors through the defining bilinearity relations of the algebraic tensor product $H\odot\mathbb C^{r}$ and is a well-defined complex-linear map ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] clause (a)). Every element of $H\odot\mathbb C^{r}$ can be written as $\sum_{l}w_{l}\otimes e_{l}$: a finite sum $\sum_{i}u_{i}\otimes z_{i}$ equals $\sum_{l}\bigl(\sum_{i}z_{i,l}u_{i}\bigr)\otimes e_{l}$ by bilinearity. For such an element, [F1] gives $\Theta_{0}(\sum_{l}w_{l}\otimes e_{l})=\sum_{l}\iota_{l}(w_{l})=(w_{1},\dots,w_{r})$ and $\|\sum_{l}w_{l}\otimes e_{l}\|^{2}=\sum_{l}\|w_{l}\|^{2} =\|\Theta_{0}(\sum_{l}w_{l}\otimes e_{l})\|^{2}_{H^{(r)}}$, so $\Theta_{0}$ is an isometry of the inner-product space $H\odot\mathbb C^{r}$ onto the dense subspace $\bigoplus_{l}H$ of $H^{(r)}$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 [Surjectivity] Let $g\in H^{(r)}$. By [F3] each component $g_{l}$ is an $L^{2}$ class and $g=(g_{1},\dots,g_{r})=\Psi_{0}((g_{l}))$; hence $\Psi_{0}$ is surjective, and (a) is proved. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F3]

2.2 [Extension and surjectivity] By [F5] the isometry $\Theta_{0}$ extends uniquely to a linear isometry $\Theta:H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}\to H^{(r)}$, because $\kappa(H\odot\mathbb C^{r})$ is dense in the completion ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] clause (c)) and $H^{(r)}$ is complete. Its image contains the dense subspace $\bigoplus_{l}H$ and is complete, hence closed in $H^{(r)}$; therefore $\Theta$ is surjective, so it is unitary. This proves (b) except for the displayed formula, which holds on elementary tensors by construction and extends to all $w$ by continuity of the bounded operators involved. [step 1.3, F1, F5, algebra]

3.1 [Intertwining identities] For $u\in H$ and $z=\sum_{l}z_{l}e_{l}$, $\Theta^{-1}\bigl(a\,\Theta(\kappa(u\otimes z))\bigr) =\Theta^{-1}\bigl(a\sum_{l}z_{l}\iota_{l}(u)\bigr) =\Theta^{-1}\bigl(\sum_{l}z_{l}\iota_{l}(au)\bigr) =\kappa(au\otimes z)=(M_{a}\otimes I)\kappa(u\otimes z)$, where the last identity is [F2]; similarly $\Theta^{-1}\bigl(T_{v}^{(r)}\Theta(\kappa(u\otimes z))\bigr) =\kappa(T_{v}u\otimes z)=(T_{v}\otimes I)\kappa(u\otimes z)$, since $T_{v}^{(r)}$ acts componentwise and $T_{v}^{(r)}\iota_{l}(u)=\iota_{l}(T_{v}u)$ ([[lem-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-momentum-operators-self-adjoint]] clause (c)). Both sides of each identity are bounded operators (the amplifications are bounded by [F2], and $\Theta$ is unitary by step 2.2), and the elementary tensors have dense span in $H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}$ [F1]; hence the identities hold on all of $H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}$. This proves (c). [step 1.3, step 2.2, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- **Two descriptions of one space.** Clause (b) says that a finite internal
  factor $\mathbb C^{r}$ may be read either as a tensor factor or as component
  bookkeeping; the component reading is the one used by the model definition on
  this page. Nothing here identifies a component index with a spatial
  direction or an observable.
- **Only bounded amplifications.** The intertwining identities of clause (c)
  use the bounded amplifications of the cited supplier; no unbounded operator
  is extended or transported by this lemma.

items.title: Componentwise position and momentum operators on the component-valued wave-function space
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the
cited scalar operator and spectral suppliers. Fix integers $d\ge1$, $r\ge1$ and
$\hbar>0$. Let $H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ be the
component-valued space of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]]
with its componentwise inner product, let $Q_{j}^{(1)},P_{k}^{(1)}$ be the
scalar position and momentum operators on $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ of
[[def-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-position-and-momentum-operators]], and let
$\mathcal F_{2}$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with
$\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^{1}$
([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Write
$\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}:=\Psi_{0}\bigl(\bigoplus_{l}\mathcal F_{2}\bigr)\Psi_{0}^{-1}$
for its componentwise version, with $\Psi_{0}$ the unitary of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] clause (a).
Define, componentwise,
$$D(Q_{j}):=\bigl\{f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}:\ x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\bigr\},\qquad (Q_{j}f)_{l}:=x_{j}f_{l},$$
$$D(P_{k}):=\bigl\{f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}:\ D_{k}f_{l}\text{ exists in }L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\bigr\},\qquad (P_{k}f)_{l}:=-i\hbar\,D_{k}f_{l},$$
where $D_{k}$ is the weak derivative of [[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]].
Write $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ for the classes whose components
lie in $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]),
and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ for the componentwise Schwartz
class ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]). Then:

(a) under $\Psi_{0}$ the operators $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are the orthogonal sums
$\bigoplus_{l}Q_{j}^{(1)}$ and $\bigoplus_{l}P_{k}^{(1)}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-orthogonal-sums-of-self-adjoint-operators]]; in particular
$Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are densely defined and self-adjoint with the displayed
domains;

(b) $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$ is unitary,
$$D(P_{k})=\bigl\{f\in H^{(r)}:\ \xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})\bigr\},$$
and for every $f\in D(P_{k})$
$$\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}(P_{k}f)(\xi)=2\pi\hbar\,\xi_{k}\,\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi;$$

(c) the componentwise translation $T_{a}^{(r)}f:=f(\cdot-a)$, $a\in\mathbb R^{d}$,
is unitary, leaves $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$,
$W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ and $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$
invariant, satisfies $D_{k}(T_{a}^{(r)}f)=T_{a}^{(r)}(D_{k}f)$ for
$f\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$, and
$$T_{a}^{(r)}D(Q_{j})=D(Q_{j}),\quad T_{a}^{(r)}Q_{j}\bigl(T_{a}^{(r)}\bigr)^{-1}=Q_{j}-a_{j}I,\qquad T_{a}^{(r)}D(P_{k})=D(P_{k}),\quad T_{a}^{(r)}P_{k}\bigl(T_{a}^{(r)}\bigr)^{-1}=P_{k};$$

(d) for every $f\in D(P_{j})$,
$$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t\bigl(T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}f-f\bigr)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}f \qquad\text{in }H^{(r)},$$
so the strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group
$t\mapsto T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}$ has generator $-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}$ and
$$T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}=\exp\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tP_{j}\Bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
the exponential being the spectral-calculus flow of the self-adjoint operator
$P_{j}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice; integers $d,r\ge1$; $\hbar>0$; the scalar operators $Q_{j}^{(1)},P_{k}^{(1)}$; the componentwise operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$; the unitaries $\Psi_{0}$ and $\mathcal F_{2},\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$; the translations $T_{a},T_{a}^{(r)}$; classes $f,g\in H^{(r)}$; a vector $a\in\mathbb R^{d}$; a real $t\ne0$; a coordinate index $j,k$.

[F1] **Scalar position and momentum.** On $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ the operators $Q_{j}^{(1)}$ and $P_{k}^{(1)}$ are self-adjoint with $D(Q_{j}^{(1)})=\{f:x_{j}f\in L^{2}\}$ and $D(P_{k}^{(1)})=\{f:\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}f\in L^{2}\}$, $\mathcal F_{2}(P_{k}^{(1)}f)(\xi)=2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}f(\xi)$ for $f\in D(P_{k}^{(1)})$, the scalar translations $T_{a}g=g(\cdot-a)$ are unitary with $T_{a}D(Q_{j}^{(1)})=D(Q_{j}^{(1)})$, $T_{a}Q_{j}^{(1)}T_{a}^{-1}=Q_{j}^{(1)}-a_{j}I$, $T_{a}D(P_{k}^{(1)})=D(P_{k}^{(1)})$, $T_{a}P_{k}^{(1)}T_{a}^{-1}=P_{k}^{(1)}$, and $T_{a}$ preserves $W^{1,2},W^{2,2}$ with $D_{k}(T_{a}g)=T_{a}(D_{k}g)$ ([[lem-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-momentum-operators-self-adjoint]] clauses (a)-(c)). For a Schwartz class the classical derivative is the weak derivative and lies in the Schwartz class ([[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]], [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]).

[F2] **Componentwise identifications.** $\Psi_{0}:\bigoplus_{l}L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)\to H^{(r)}$ is a unitary isomorphism, a tuple of classes is mapped to the class of its component function, and the componentwise multipliers and translations of $H^{(r)}$ correspond under $\Psi_{0}$ to the amplifications $M_{a}\otimes I$ and $T_{a}\otimes I$ ([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] clauses (a),(c)). In particular a class in $H^{(r)}$ has all its components in the Schwartz class exactly when it lies in $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]).

[F3] **Orthogonal sums.** For finitely many densely defined self-adjoint operators $A_{l}$ the orthogonal sum $\bigoplus_{l}A_{l}$ is self-adjoint with domain $\{(x_{l}):x_{l}\in D(A_{l}),\ \sum_{l}\|A_{l}x_{l}\|^{2}<\infty\}$, and the orthogonal sum of unitaries is unitary with norm one ([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-orthogonal-sums-of-self-adjoint-operators]] clauses (b),(c)).

[F4] **Plancherel and multipliers.** $\mathcal F_{2}$ is unitary ([[thm-plancherel]]); for $L^{2}$ classes $u,w$ with $-i\hbar D_{k}$ defined componentwise, the Fourier multiplier identity is $\mathcal F_{2}(D_{k}u)(\xi)=2\pi i\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}u(\xi)$ for classes whose weak derivative is in $L^{2}$ ([[lem-weak-derivatives-are-polynomial-fourier-multipliers]]); the scalar function $\mathcal F_{2}(T_{a}u)(\xi)=e^{-2\pi ia\cdot\xi}\mathcal F_{2}u(\xi)$ holds for $u\in L^{1}\cap L^{2}$ and extends by density; the exponential is entire with derivative itself, so $\frac{e^{i\theta}-1}{\theta}\to i$ as $\theta\to0$, and $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]; the bound follows from the mean value estimate for the curve $s\mapsto e^{is\theta}$ over $[0,1]$ with $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$). Translation depends norm-continuously on $a$ in $L^{2}$, so $a\mapsto T_{a}^{(r)}$ is strongly continuous ([[lem-complex-translation-and-approximate-identity-interfaces]]). [F4]

[F5] **Generation and uniqueness.** For a self-adjoint $T$ the family $t\mapsto e^{itT}$ is a strongly continuous unitary group with generator $iT$, and two strongly continuous unitary groups with one and the same generator agree ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]], [[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]], [[def-infinitesimal-generator-of-a-unitary-group]], [[thm-stone-one-parameter-unitary-groups]]).

[F6] **Dominated convergence.** If $|h_{t}|\le G$ with $G$ integrable and $h_{t}\to h$ pointwise as $t\to0$, then $\int|h_{t}-h|\to0$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; transport the componentwise operators to orthogonal sums of scalar operators, read off self-adjointness and the Fourier representation, verify the translation identities componentwise and prove the difference-quotient limit by Plancherel with dominated convergence before identifying the group.

**Given:** The data of the statement and [F1]-[F6].

1.1 [Operators as orthogonal sums] Let $f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}$. By [F2] one has $\Psi_{0}^{-1}f=(f_{l})\in\bigoplus_{l}L^{2}$, and $f\in D(Q_{j})$ holds exactly when $x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}$ for every $l$, that is when $\Psi_{0}^{-1}f\in\bigoplus_{l}D(Q_{j}^{(1)})$; on that domain $\Psi_{0}^{-1}(Q_{j}f)=(x_{j}f_{l})_{l}=(\bigoplus_{l}Q_{j}^{(1)})\Psi_{0}^{-1}f$. The same computation with $D_{k}f_{l}$ in place of $x_{j}f_{l}$ gives $\Psi_{0}^{-1}(P_{k}f)=(\bigoplus_{l}P_{k}^{(1)})\Psi_{0}^{-1}f$ on $\Psi_{0}^{-1}D(P_{k})=\bigoplus_{l}D(P_{k}^{(1)})$. The finite-sum condition in the domain of an orthogonal sum is automatic here: if every $\|Q_{j}^{(1)}f_{l}\|$ is finite then $\sum_{l}\|Q_{j}^{(1)}f_{l}\|^{2}=\|Q_{j}f\|^{2}<\infty$, and similarly for $P_{k}$. This proves the identification in (a). [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 [A scalar difference quotient] Let $g\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ with $\xi_{j}\mathcal F_{2}g\in L^{2}$, that is $g\in D(P_{j}^{(1)})$ by [F1], and let $t\ne0$. The modulation identity $\mathcal F_{2}(T_{te_{j}}g)(\xi)=e^{-2\pi it\xi_{j}}\mathcal F_{2}g(\xi)$ of [F4] gives $\mathcal F_{2}\Bigl(\frac1t\bigl(T_{te_{j}}g-g\bigr)\Bigr)(\xi) =\frac{e^{-2\pi it\xi_{j}}-1}{t}\,\mathcal F_{2}g(\xi).$ Writing $\theta:=-2\pi t\xi_{j}$, the factor equals $\frac{e^{i\theta}-1}{i\theta}\cdot\bigl(-2\pi i\xi_{j}\bigr)$; by [F4] the first factor tends to $1$ and $\theta\to0$ for every fixed $\xi$ as $t\to0$, so the pointwise limit of the right-hand side is $-2\pi i\xi_{j}\mathcal F_{2}g(\xi)=\mathcal F_{2}(-D_{j}g)(\xi)$ [F4]. For domination, [F4] gives $|\frac{e^{i\theta}-1}{t}|\le|\theta/t|=2\pi|\xi_{j}|$, so the modulus of the difference $\bigl(\frac{e^{-2\pi it\xi_{j}}-1}{t}+2\pi i\xi_{j}\bigr)\mathcal F_{2}g(\xi)$ is at most $4\pi|\xi_{j}|\,|\mathcal F_{2}g(\xi)|$, whose square is integrable because $\xi_{j}\mathcal F_{2}g\in L^{2}$. Hence [F6] gives $\mathcal F_{2}\bigl(\frac1t(T_{te_{j}}g-g)\bigr)\to\mathcal F_{2}(-D_{j}g)$ in $L^{2}$; since $\mathcal F_{2}$ is a surjective isometry [F4], and $D_{j}g=-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}^{(1)}g$, this yields $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t\bigl(T_{te_{j}}g-g\bigr)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}^{(1)}g \qquad\text{in }L^{2}.$ [F1, F4, F6, algebra]

2.1 [Self-adjointness] Each scalar $Q_{j}^{(1)}$ and $P_{k}^{(1)}$ is self-adjoint by [F1], so [F3] makes their finite orthogonal sums self-adjoint with the displayed domains and dense domains; by step 1.1 these sums are the conjugates of $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ by the unitary $\Psi_{0}$, hence $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are densely defined and self-adjoint. This completes (a). [step 1.1, F1, F3]

2.2 [Fourier representation] By [F2] and [F3], $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$ is the orthogonal sum of the unitaries $\mathcal F_{2}$, hence unitary. For $f\in D(P_{k})$ its components satisfy $\mathcal F_{2}(P_{k}^{(1)}f_{l})(\xi)=2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}f_{l}(\xi)$ for almost every $\xi$ by [F1]; assembling components gives $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}(P_{k}f)(\xi)=2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f(\xi)$ for almost every $\xi$. The domain description follows because $\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}f_{l}\in L^{2}$ for all $l$ is exactly $\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$. This proves (b). [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.3 [Translation identities] By [F2] the translation $T_{a}^{(r)}$ corresponds to $\bigoplus_{l}T_{a}$, which is unitary by [F3] and [F1]; it preserves the componentwise Schwartz and Sobolev classes because each scalar $T_{a}$ does [F1]. The identities $D_{k}(T_{a}^{(r)}f)=T_{a}^{(r)}(D_{k}f)$ and $T_{a}^{(r)}D(Q_{j})=D(Q_{j})$, $T_{a}^{(r)}Q_{j}(T_{a}^{(r)})^{-1}=Q_{j}-a_{j}I$, $T_{a}^{(r)}P_{k}(T_{a}^{(r)})^{-1}=P_{k}$ are componentwise instances of [F1]; for instance, $(T_{a}^{(r)}Q_{j}(T_{a}^{(r)})^{-1}f)_{l} =T_{a}(x_{j}T_{-a}f_{l})=(x_{j}-a_{j})f_{l}$ for $f_{l}\in D(Q_{j}^{(1)})$, and the domain equality follows from the scalar one. This proves (c). [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.4 [The componentwise limit] Let $f\in D(P_{j})$. Applying step 1.2 to each component $f_{l}\in D(P_{j}^{(1)})$ and assembling components through the unitary $\Psi_{0}$ [F2] gives $\frac1t(T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}f-f)\to\bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}^{(1)}f_{l}\bigr)_{l} =-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}f$ in $H^{(r)}$ as $t\to0$; this is the first assertion of (d). [step 1.2, F1, F2, algebra]

3.1 [The group of translations and its generator] Fix $j$. The family $U_{j}(t):=T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group: the group law and unitarity follow from the componentwise definition of translations and [F3], and strong continuity from [F4]. By step 2.4 its generator $G$ satisfies $G\supseteq-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}$; by [F5] applied to the self-adjoint operator $T:=-P_{j}/\hbar$, the family $V_{j}(t):=\exp\bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tP_{j}\bigr)=\exp(itT)$ is a strongly continuous unitary group with generator $iT=-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}$ and domain $D(P_{j})$, and it preserves $D(P_{j})$ [F5]. On $D(P_{j})$ both groups have the same right derivative at $0$, and both preserve $D(P_{j})$; hence $w(t):=U_{j}(t)g-V_{j}(t)g$ for fixed $g\in D(P_{j})$ satisfies $w'(t)=\bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}\bigr)w(t)$ and $\frac{d}{dt}\|w(t)\|^{2}=2\operatorname{Re}\langle w(t),-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}w(t)\rangle=0$ because $\langle P_{j}w(t),w(t)\rangle$ is real; with $w(0)=0$ this gives $U_{j}(t)g=V_{j}(t)g$ for all $t$ on the dense set $D(P_{j})$, hence $U_{j}(t)=V_{j}(t)$ by continuity and unitarity. This proves (d). [step 2.4, F1, F5, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- **Domains are part of the statement.** $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are unbounded;
  clause (a) exhibits them as orthogonal sums with maximal componentwise
  domains, and no product or commutator of two such operators is asserted
  here beyond the domains displayed.
- **The difference-quotient clause is the generator statement.** Clause (d)
  identifies the coordinate translation group with the spectral flow of the
  momentum component; it is used by the physics items of this page to read the
  translation unitaries as generated by momentum, and no global exponential
  $\exp(-ia\cdot P/\hbar)$ for a vector $a$ is asserted in this lemma beyond
  the displayed coordinate statement.

items.title: Canonical commutation relations on the component-valued core and commutation with the internal factor
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix integers $d\ge1$,
$r\ge1$ and $\hbar>0$, let $H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ with
the componentwise position and momentum operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]], let
$\mathcal S^{(r)}:=\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ be the componentwise
Schwartz class ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]), and let $\Psi_{0}$
and $\Theta$ be the unitaries of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]]. For
$S=(S_{lm})\in M_{r}(\mathbb C)$ write
$$S_{\times}f:=\Bigl(\sum_{m=1}^{r}S_{lm}f_{m}\Bigr)_{l}\qquad(f\in H^{(r)}).$$
Then:

(a) $\mathcal S^{(r)}\subseteq D(Q_{j})\cap D(P_{k})$ for all $j,k$,
$Q_{j}\mathcal S^{(r)}\subseteq\mathcal S^{(r)}$ and
$P_{k}\mathcal S^{(r)}\subseteq\mathcal S^{(r)}$, and on $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ the
canonical commutation relations hold:
$$(Q_{j}P_{k}-P_{k}Q_{j})f=i\hbar\,\delta_{jk}f\qquad(f\in\mathcal S^{(r)});$$

(b) $S_{\times}$ is bounded with $\|S_{\times}\|=\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}$
([[def-operator-norm]]), and
$$S_{\times}D(Q_{j})\subseteq D(Q_{j}),\quad Q_{j}S_{\times}f=S_{\times}Q_{j}f\ (f\in D(Q_{j})),\qquad S_{\times}D(P_{k})\subseteq D(P_{k}),\quad P_{k}S_{\times}f=S_{\times}P_{k}f\ (f\in D(P_{k}));$$

(c) the spectral projection-valued measures of $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are
$$E_{Q_{j}}(B)=M_{\mathbf 1_{x_{j}^{-1}(B)}},\qquad E_{P_{k}}(B)=\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)*}M_{\mathbf 1_{\{2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}\in B\}}}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)} \qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel}),$$
where $M_{g}$ is multiplication by $g$; consequently
$S_{\times}E_{Q_{j}}(B)=E_{Q_{j}}(B)S_{\times}$ and
$S_{\times}E_{P_{k}}(B)=E_{P_{k}}(B)S_{\times}$ for every Borel $B$, and for
unitary $V\in U(r)$ and every $f\in H^{(r)}$
$$\bigl\|E_{Q_{j}}(B)V_{\times}f\bigr\|=\bigl\|E_{Q_{j}}(B)f\bigr\|,\qquad \bigl\|E_{P_{k}}(B)V_{\times}f\bigr\|=\bigl\|E_{P_{k}}(B)f\bigr\|;$$

(d) under the tensor identification $\Theta$ the operator $S_{\times}$
corresponds to the bounded amplification $I\otimes S$ of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], that is
$\Theta^{-1}S_{\times}\Theta=I\otimes S$; in particular the internal-factor
operators commute with the spatial ones in the sense of (b).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice; integers $d,r\ge1$; $\hbar>0$; the componentwise operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$ and their scalar counterparts $Q_{j}^{(1)},P_{k}^{(1)}$; the unitaries $\Psi_{0},\Theta$ and the componentwise Plancherel transform $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$; a matrix $S\in M_{r}(\mathbb C)$; classes $f\in H^{(r)}$ and $u\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$; Borel sets $B\subseteq\mathbb R$.

[F1] **Scalar CCR on the core.** $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)\subseteq D(Q_{j}^{(1)})\cap D(P_{k}^{(1)})$, the scalar operators map the scalar Schwartz class into itself, and $(Q_{j}^{(1)}P_{k}^{(1)}-P_{k}^{(1)}Q_{j}^{(1)})u=i\hbar\delta_{jk}u$ for scalar Schwartz classes $u$ ([[lem-nrqm-framework-ccr-on-the-schwartz-core]] clauses (a),(b)).

[F2] **Componentwise operators and their identification.** $Q_{j},P_{k}$ are the orthogonal sums of the scalar operators under $\Psi_{0}$, they are self-adjoint with their maximal componentwise domains, and $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$ is unitary with the Fourier representation of $P_{k}$ ([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clauses (a),(b)); the bounded multipliers and translations correspond to the amplifications of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] clause (c).

[F3] **Weak derivatives are linear.** If $f_{1},\dots,f_{r}\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ have weak derivatives $D_{k}f_{m}\in L^{2}$ and $\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{r}\in\mathbb C$, then $\sum_{m}\alpha_{m}f_{m}$ has weak derivative $\sum_{m}\alpha_{m}D_{k}f_{m}$: the defining integration-by-parts identity is verified term by term against test functions ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]).

[F4] **Multiplier spectral measure and uniqueness.** For a $\sigma$-finite measure space and a real measurable finite-valued multiplier $m$, the multiplication operator $M_{m}$ is self-adjoint with regular spectral PVM $E(B)=M_{\mathbf 1_{m^{-1}(B)}}$, and its law is $\|E(B)\psi\|^{2}=\int_{m^{-1}(B)}|\psi|^{2}$ ([[lem-nrqm-observables-l2-multiplication-spectral-measure]] clauses (a)-(c), [[def-projection-valued-measure]]). A regular PVM representing a self-adjoint operator is its spectral PVM ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]). Integrals of nonnegative product-measurable functions may be iterated ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); dominated convergence for the componentwise strong additivity is [[thm-dominated-convergence]].

[F5] **Bounded matrix action.** For $S\in M_{r}(\mathbb C)$ and $f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$, $\|Sf(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|f(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}$ pointwise ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]]), so $S_{\times}$ is bounded with $\|S_{\times}\|\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}$; every elementary tensor $\kappa(u\otimes z)$ satisfies $(I\otimes S)\kappa(u\otimes z)=\kappa(u\otimes Sz)$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] clause (a)).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; assemble the scalar core identities componentwise, verify the linear-algebra commutation for matrix multipliers from the definitions of the weak derivative, transport the scalar spectral measures through the unitaries, and identify the amplification on elementary tensors.

**Given:** The data of the statement and [F1]-[F5].

1.1 [The core and the CCR] For $u=(u_{l})\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$ each component $u_{l}$ is a scalar Schwartz class, so $u_{l}\in D(Q_{j}^{(1)})\cap D(P_{k}^{(1)})$ and $Q_{j}^{(1)}u_{l},P_{k}^{(1)}u_{l}\in\mathcal S$ by [F1]; hence $u\in D(Q_{j})\cap D(P_{k})$ and $Q_{j}u=(Q_{j}^{(1)}u_{l})_{l}$, $P_{k}u=(P_{k}^{(1)}u_{l})_{l}$ lie in $\mathcal S^{(r)}$. Applying the scalar relation [F1] componentwise gives $(Q_{j}P_{k}-P_{k}Q_{j})u=i\hbar\delta_{jk}u$ as classes. This proves (a). [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 [Linearity of the matrix action] For $f\in D(Q_{j})$ and every $m$, $x_{j}f_{m}\in L^{2}$, so the components $x_{j}(S_{\times}f)_{l}=x_{j}\sum_{m}S_{lm}f_{m}=\sum_{m}S_{lm}x_{j}f_{m}$ are $L^{2}$ classes (finite sums), and $S_{\times}f\in D(Q_{j})$. For $f\in D(P_{k})$, [F3] applied to the finite linear combinations $\sum_{m}S_{lm}f_{m}$ gives $D_{k}(S_{\times}f)_{l}=\sum_{m}S_{lm}D_{k}f_{m}$, so $S_{\times}f\in D(P_{k})$; the actions agree with the matrix action on each component, whence $Q_{j}S_{\times}f=S_{\times}Q_{j}f$ and $P_{k}S_{\times}f=S_{\times}P_{k}f$. [F3, F2, algebra]

1.3 [The position spectral measure] Put $E(B):=M_{\mathbf 1_{x_{j}^{-1}(B)}}$ on $H^{(r)}$, the componentwise multiplication by the bounded indicator. Each $E(B)$ is an orthogonal projection and $E$ is a regular PVM: multiplicativity $E(B)E(C)=E(B\cap C)$ and the endpoint values are pointwise, and for pairwise disjoint Borel $B_{n}$ with union $B$ the strong additivity follows from $\|E(B)x-\sum_{n\le N}E(B_{n})x\|^{2} =\int\bigl|\mathbf 1_{B}-\sum_{n\le N}\mathbf 1_{B_{n}}\bigr|(x_{j})\,\|x\|^{2}\to0$ by [F4]. For $x\in D(Q_{j})$ and $y\in H^{(r)}$, the scalar pairing measure is $E_{x,y}(B)=\int_{x_{j}^{-1}(B)}\langle x(z),y(z)\rangle_{\mathbb C^{r}}\,dz$, which is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, so Tonelli gives $\int\lambda\,dE_{x,y}(\lambda)=\int x_{j}(z)\langle x(z),y(z)\rangle\,dz =\langle Q_{j}x,y\rangle$, the interchange being justified by $\int|x_{j}|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|<\infty$; and $\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{x}(\lambda)=\int x_{j}^{2}\|x\|^{2}$ is finite exactly when $x\in D(Q_{j})$. Hence $E$ represents $Q_{j}$, and by uniqueness [F4] it is the spectral PVM of $Q_{j}$. [F4, F2, algebra]

2.1 [Norm of the matrix action] [F5] gives the pointwise bound $\|S_{\times}f(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|f(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}$, so $\|S_{\times}f\|_{H^{(r)}}\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|f\|_{H^{(r)}}$ and $\|S_{\times}\|\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Choose a unit vector $z_{0}\in\mathbb C^{r}$ with $\|Sz_{0}\|=\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}$, and a unit $h\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ with $\|h\|=1$; then $f=h\,z_{0}$ (the class $x\mapsto h(x)z_{0}$) has $\|f\|_{H^{(r)}}=\|h\|\,\|z_{0}\|=1$ and $\|S_{\times}f\|_{H^{(r)}}=\|h\|\,\|Sz_{0}\|=\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}$, so $\|S_{\times}\|=\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}$; this proves the norm statement of (b), and step 1.2 is the commutation statement. [step 1.2, F5, algebra]

2.2 [The momentum spectral measure] Put $E'(B):=\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)*}M_{\mathbf 1_{\{2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}\in B\}}}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$, the unitary conjugate of the multiplication PVM by the scalar multiplier $2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}$; conjugating an orthogonal projection by a unitary gives an orthogonal projection and conjugation preserves products and strong sums, so $E'$ is a regular PVM. For $x\in D(P_{k})$ put $g:=\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}x$ and for $y'\in H^{(r)}$ put $h':=\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}y'$; by [F2] and the defining conjugation, $E'_{x,y'}(B)=\int_{\{2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}\in B\}}\langle g(\xi),h'(\xi)\rangle\,d\xi$, so Tonelli gives $\int\lambda\,dE'_{x,y'}(\lambda)=\int 2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}\langle g,h'\rangle =\langle 2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}g,h'\rangle=\langle P_{k}x,y'\rangle$, using the Fourier representation [F2]; and $\int\lambda^{2}dE'_{x}(\lambda) =\|\xi\mapsto2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}g(\xi)\|^{2}$ is finite exactly when $x\in D(P_{k})$. Hence $E'$ represents $P_{k}$, and by uniqueness [F4] it is the spectral PVM of $P_{k}$. [step 1.3, F2, F4, algebra]

3.1 [Commutation with the spectral measures] The multiplier $M_{\mathbf 1_{x_{j}^{-1}(B)}}$ commutes with $S_{\times}$ because both are multiplication by functions on the finite-dimensional values: pointwise, $\mathbf 1_{x_{j}^{-1}(B)}(x)Sz=S(\mathbf 1_{x_{j}^{-1}(B)}(x)z)$ for every $z\in\mathbb C^{r}$. For the momentum case, $S_{\times}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}=\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}S_{\times}$ because $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$ acts on components and matrix multiplication acts on the finite index, so $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}\bigl(S_{\times}g\bigr) =\bigl(\sum_{m}S_{lm}\mathcal F_{2}g_{m}\bigr)_{l}=S_{\times}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}g$; and $S_{\times}$ commutes with the scalar multiplier by the same pointwise argument. Hence $S_{\times}$ commutes with both $E_{Q_{j}}(B)$ and $E_{P_{k}}(B)$ by steps 1.3 and 2.2. For unitary $V\in U(r)$ and $f\in H^{(r)}$, $V_{\times}$ is unitary (it is matrix multiplication by a unitary pointwise) and commutes with the PVMs, so $\|E(B)V_{\times}f\|=\|V_{\times}E(B)f\|=\|E(B)f\|$, which is the last assertion of (c). [step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.2, F2, algebra]

4.1 [Amplification] Let $u\in H$ and $z=\sum_{l}z_{l}e_{l}\in\mathbb C^{r}$, and put $w:=\Theta(\kappa(u\otimes z))$; by [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] clause (b), $w=\sum_{l}z_{l}\iota_{l}(u)$, where $\iota_{l}(u)\in H^{(r)}$ denotes the vector with $u$ in slot $l$ and $0$ elsewhere. Then $\Theta^{-1}S_{\times}\Theta\,\kappa(u\otimes z)=\Theta^{-1}\bigl(S_{\times}w\bigr)$, and $S_{\times}w=\sum_{l}z_{l}S_{\times}\iota_{l}(u)=\sum_{l,m}z_{l}S_{ml}\iota_{m}(u)$; applying $\Theta^{-1}$ with clause (b) gives $\sum_{l,m}z_{l}S_{ml}\kappa(u\otimes e_{m})=\kappa(u\otimes Sz)$, where the last step expands $Sz=\sum_{m}\bigl(\sum_{l}S_{ml}z_{l}\bigr)e_{m}$; by [F5] this equals $(I\otimes S)\kappa(u\otimes z)$. Both sides are bounded operators ([[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] clause (a) and step 2.1) that agree on the elementary tensors, whose span is dense in $H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] clause (c)); hence $\Theta^{-1}S_{\times}\Theta=I\otimes S$, which is (d). [step 2.1, F5, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- **Only the core carries the CCR.** Clause (a) is a relation on the common
  Schwartz core; no product of the unbounded operators is claimed to be
  defined on all of $H^{(r)}$, and the companion counterexample of this page
  shows that no bounded-operator form with nonzero commutator can hold.
- **The internal factor is a bookkeeping factor.** Clause (d) says that the
  matrix action is exactly the amplification $I\otimes S$; together with (c)
  it says that the spatial spectral measures are invariant under the action of
  the internal factor, so the spatial laws do not distinguish internal
  components. No identification of the internal factor with a spatial object
  is made.

J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Section 2.3, printed pages 24-28 (PDF pages 32-36): the commutator [x,p]=i hbar in the position representation and its role in the operator calculus

items.title: The momentum representation of the componentwise kinematics
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix $d\ge1$, $r\ge1$ and
$\hbar>0$, let $H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ with the
componentwise operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]], let $U$ be the
unitary of [[lem-nrqm-composites-momentum-fourier-jacobian]] clause (c), which
on Schwartz classes acts by
$$(U\psi)(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^{d}}e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar}\psi(x)\,dx,$$
and put $U^{(r)}:=\Psi_{0}\bigl(\bigoplus_{l}U\bigr)\Psi_{0}^{-1}$ with
$\Psi_{0}$ as in [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]].
Then:

(a) $U^{(r)}:L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d},dx;\mathbb C^{r})\to L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d},dp;\mathbb C^{r})$
is unitary; for $f=(f_{l})\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$,
$$(U^{(r)}f)_{l}(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^{d}}e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar}f_{l}(x)\,dx \qquad(l=1,\dots,r),$$
$U^{(r)}f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$, and
$\int_{\mathbb R^{d}}\|U^{(r)}f(p)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}^{2}\,dp
=\int_{\mathbb R^{d}}\|f(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}^{2}\,dx$;

(b) $U^{(r)}D(P_{k})=D(M_{p_{k}})$, where $M_{p_{k}}g(p):=p_{k}g(p)$ on
$D(M_{p_{k}})=\{g\in L^{2}(dp;\mathbb C^{r}):p_{k}g\in L^{2}\}$, and
$$U^{(r)}P_{k}=M_{p_{k}}U^{(r)};$$
equivalently $(U^{(r)}P_{k}f)(p)=p_{k}(U^{(r)}f)(p)$ for every $f\in D(P_{k})$
and almost every $p$;

(c) for every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ and every $j$,
$$U^{(r)}(Q_{j}f)(p)=i\hbar\,\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{j}}\bigl(U^{(r)}f\bigr)(p) \qquad(p\in\mathbb R^{d}),$$
and both sides are Schwartz classes; no identity of unbounded operators on the
full domain of $Q_{j}$ is asserted;

(d) for every $a\in\mathbb R^{d}$, with $T_{a}^{(r)}$ the componentwise
translation of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]]
clause (c),
$$U^{(r)}T_{a}^{(r)}U^{(r)-1}=M_{e^{-ia\cdot p/\hbar}},$$
the bounded multiplication operator by the unimodular function
$p\mapsto e^{-ia\cdot p/\hbar}$;

(e) under $\Psi_{0}$ the operator $U^{(r)}$ is the orthogonal sum
$\bigoplus_{l}U$; no physical identification of $U^{(r)}f$ with a measured
momentum distribution is made by this lemma.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice; integers $d,r\ge1$; $\hbar>0$; the scalar unitary $U$ and its componentwise version $U^{(r)}$; the operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$ and their scalar counterparts; a class $f=(f_{l})$; a vector $a\in\mathbb R^{d}$; indices $j,k$.

[F1] **The scalar momentum representation.** $U$ is a unitary $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d},dx)\to L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d},dp)$ with the displayed Schwartz formula; $U=D_{\hbar}\mathcal F_{2}$ on Schwartz classes, where $D_{\hbar}g(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-d/2}g(p/(2\pi\hbar))$ is a surjective isometry of $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ and $\mathcal F_{2}$ is the unitary Plancherel transform of [[thm-plancherel]]; and on Schwartz classes $U$ acts as the topological automorphism $D_{\hbar}\mathcal F_{2}$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-momentum-fourier-jacobian]] clauses (a)-(c), [[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]]).

[F2] **Scalar domains, Fourier representation and translations.** $D(P_{k}^{(1)})=\{f:\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}f\in L^{2}\}$ and $\mathcal F_{2}(P_{k}^{(1)}f)(\xi)=2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}f(\xi)$; the scalar translations are unitary and satisfy $\mathcal F_{2}(T_{a}f)(\xi)=e^{-2\pi ia\cdot\xi}\mathcal F_{2}f(\xi)$ on $L^{1}\cap L^{2}$, hence on $L^{2}$ by density and continuity ([[lem-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-momentum-operators-self-adjoint]] clauses (b),(c), [[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]]).

[F3] **Componentwise operators and identifications.** $\Psi_{0}$ is unitary and $Q_{j},P_{k}$ are its conjugates of the corresponding orthogonal sums; $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$ is unitary with the componentwise multiplication representation of $P_{k}$; the componentwise translations are the conjugates of $\bigoplus_{l}T_{a}$ ([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clauses (a)-(c), [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] clauses (a),(c)).

[F4] **Differentiation under the integral.** If for a parameter $p$ the integrand is differentiable with derivative dominated by an integrable function independent of the parameter, the derivative may be taken under the integral sign ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]). Change of variables under a translation holds for integrable functions ([[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]]). Tonelli's theorem for nonnegative measurable integrands ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F5] **Dense extension of bounded identities.** If two bounded operators agree on a dense subspace, they agree everywhere ([[thm-extension-of-a-bounded-map-from-a-dense-subspace]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; reduce unitarity and the Schwartz formula to the scalar supplier through the orthogonal-sum identification, transport the momentum representation and its domain, differentiate the Schwartz transform under the integral for the core identity of position, and extend the translation conjugation by density.

**Given:** The data of the statement and [F1]-[F5].

1.1 [Unitarity, Schwartz formula and Plancherel identity] By [F3] and [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-orthogonal-sums-of-self-adjoint-operators]] clause (c) the orthogonal sum $\bigoplus_{l}U$ is unitary, hence so is its conjugate $U^{(r)}$ by the unitary $\Psi_{0}$. On a Schwartz class $f=(f_{l})$ each component is a scalar Schwartz class, so [F1] gives $(U^{(r)}f)_{l}=Uf_{l}$ with the displayed integral formula and $Uf_{l}\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$; hence $U^{(r)}f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$. The Plancherel identity is the componentwise scalar identity of [F1], summed over $l$ (finite sum) and read with the componentwise norms. This proves (a) and (e). [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 [Momentum domain and action] Let $f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}$. By [F2], for each $l$ one has $f_{l}\in D(P_{k}^{(1)})$ exactly when $\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}f_{l}\in L^{2}$, and then $\mathcal F_{2}(P_{k}^{(1)}f_{l})=2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}f_{l}$. Since $U=D_{\hbar}\mathcal F_{2}$ and $p_{k}D_{\hbar}h=D_{\hbar}(2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}h)$ pointwise for every $h\in L^{2}$ with $\xi_{k}h\in L^{2}$, one gets $p_{k}Uf_{l}=U(P_{k}^{(1)}f_{l})$ and, conversely, $p_{k}Uf_{l}\in L^{2}$ exactly when $\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}f_{l}\in L^{2}$ because $D_{\hbar}$ is an isometry; thus $UD(P_{k}^{(1)})=D(M_{p_{k}})$ and $UP_{k}^{(1)}=M_{p_{k}}U$. Assembling components through $\Psi_{0}$ [F3] gives $U^{(r)}D(P_{k})=D(M_{p_{k}})$ and $U^{(r)}P_{k}=M_{p_{k}}U^{(r)}$, which is (b). [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.2 [Position in the momentum representation] Let $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ and consider one component $f_{l}\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$. The function $p\mapsto e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar}x_{j}f_{l}(x)$ is, for fixed $x$, the $p_{j}$-derivative of $e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar}f_{l}(x)$, and for $p$ in a compact set its modulus is bounded by $(1+|x|)|f_{l}(x)|$, which is integrable; [F4] therefore permits differentiation under the integral, giving $\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{j}}(Uf_{l})(p) =(2\pi\hbar)^{-d/2}\int e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar}\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}x_{j}\Bigr)f_{l}(x)\,dx =\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}\Bigr)\bigl(U(Q_{j}^{(1)}f_{l})\bigr)(p),$ that is $U(Q_{j}^{(1)}f_{l})=i\hbar\partial_{p_{j}}(Uf_{l})$. Since $Uf_{l}\in\mathcal S$ by [F1], its partial derivative is again Schwartz ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]), and assembling components through [F3] proves (c). [step 1.1, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

3.1 [Translations] Let $f=(f_{l})$ be a Schwartz class and fix $a$. For each component, the substitution $y=x-a$ and [F4] give $(U T_{a}f_{l})(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-d/2}\int e^{-ip\cdot(x+a)/\hbar}f_{l}(x)\,dx =e^{-ia\cdot p/\hbar}(Uf_{l})(p)$, so $U^{(r)}T_{a}^{(r)}=M_{e^{-ia\cdot p/\hbar}}U^{(r)}$ on the dense Schwartz subspace of $H^{(r)}$; both sides are bounded operators (products of unitaries, a translation and a unimodular multiplier), so [F5] extends the identity to all of $H^{(r)}$ and $U^{(r)}T_{a}^{(r)}U^{(r)-1}=M_{e^{-ia\cdot p/\hbar}}$, which is (d). [step 1.1, F1, F3, F4, F5, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- **What the momentum representative is.** $U^{(r)}f$ is a class in
  $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d},dp;\mathbb C^{r})$ obtained from $f$ by the unitary
  transform of clause (a); the lemma makes no statement about measuring it,
  and the physical reading of $\|U^{(r)}f(p)\|^{2}dp$ as an outcome density is
  a separate consequence of the observable postulate, proved with the physics
  items of this page.
- **Core only for position.** Clause (c) is asserted on Schwartz classes, where
  both sides are ordinary functions; no claim is made that the mapping
  $g\mapsto i\hbar\partial_{p_{j}}g$ with its maximal $L^{2}$ domain is the
  unitary conjugate of the full position operator.

items.title: The massive spin-s particle model of the framework: state space, operators, units and frame readings
items.statement:
**(a) Adopted model and state space.** Adopt the kinematics and
massive-particle model postulate P5 for a declared particle of mass parameter
$m>0$, spin label $s\in\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$ and internal factor
assigned as in the identical-particle and spin postulate P6
([[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]]). Put $r:=2s+1$ and take
as the model's one-particle state space the complex Hilbert space
$$H_{s}:=L^{2}\bigl(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r}\bigr) =\Bigl\{f:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb C^{r}\ \text{measurable}:\ \int_{\mathbb R^{3}}\|f(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}^{2}\,dx<\infty\Bigr\}\Big/\!\sim,$$
the quotient by equality almost everywhere, with inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}\sum_{l=1}^{r}f_{l}\overline{g_{l}}\,dx$
linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
Thus an element of $H_{s}$ is a class of functions, not a function, and
pointwise values of a state are not defined; the position density is read from
the class through the observables of clause (b) and the observable and
probability postulate P2 ([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]],
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]). Its dimension
in the conventions of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] clause (d)1
is $\ell^{-3/2}$ per component. P5 presents the same space as the completed
tensor product $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)\widehat\otimes\mathbb C^{r}$
with the spin factor carrying the representation of P6; the unitary
identification of the two descriptions and the componentwise reading of
componentwise operators are those of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] and
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]]. The orthonormal
basis $(e_{m})_{m=-s,\dots,s}$ of $\mathbb C^{r}$ is the basis fixed by P6
([[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]] clause (ii)).

**(b) Position and momentum.** The model's $j$-th position and $k$-th momentum
are the componentwise operators $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clause (a): for
$f=(f_{l})$, restricted to the classes with $x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}$ respectively
with $D_{k}f_{l}\in L^{2}$ for all $l$,
$$(Q_{j}f)_{l}(x):=x_{j}f_{l}(x),\qquad (P_{k}f)_{l}:=-i\hbar\,D_{k}f_{l},$$
with $D_{k}$ the weak derivative and $\hbar$ the action constant of
[[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. These are the scalar operators of
[[def-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-position-and-momentum-operators]] applied
componentwise. The model assigns to $(Q_{j},\mathrm m)$ and to
$(P_{k},\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}})$ the status of assigned sharp observables in
the sense of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]
clause (a), with the units of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]
clause (d)4; both are densely defined and self-adjoint by
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clause (a). On the
Schwartz core they satisfy the componentwise canonical commutation relations,
and they commute with the internal-factor operators of clause (c) in the sense
of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-ccr-and-internal-factor-commutation]] clauses (a),(c).

**(c) Internal factor.** For $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ let $S_{i}=\hbar J_{i}$ be the
self-adjoint endomorphisms of $\mathbb C^{r}$ of the spin assignment P6
([[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]] clause (ii),
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]]), and let the model read
them on $H_{s}$ as the matrix actions
$$(S_{i}f)_{l}:=\sum_{m=1}^{r}(J_{i})_{lm}f_{m}\qquad(l=1,\dots,r),$$
that is, as the amplifications $I\otimes S_{i}$ under the tensor
identification of clause (a) ([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-ccr-and-internal-factor-commutation]]
clause (d)). Their declared unit is the unit of action ([[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]
clause (d)4). The factor is internal bookkeeping: it is not a spatial
coordinate, not a rotating body and not a relativistic spinor, and the model
assigns no position or worldline to it.

**(d) Momentum-space representative.** With $U^{(s)}$ the unitary of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-momentum-representation]] for $r=2s+1$, the
**momentum-space representative** of a preparation vector $\psi\in H_{s}$ is
$\psi_{p}:=U^{(s)}\psi\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3},dp;\mathbb C^{r})$; for a
Schwartz class $\psi$ it is the componentwise Fourier transform
$$(\psi_{p})_{l}(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar}\psi_{l}(x)\,dx,$$
and its dimension is $(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}})^{-3/2}$ per component
([[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] clause (d)2). By
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-momentum-representation]] clause (b), $P_{k}$ acts on the
momentum representative by multiplication by $p_{k}$; this is the model's
momentum reading and no measured momentum distribution is identified with
$|\psi_{p}|^{2}$ by this definition.

**(e) Frame reading.** The model's inertial frames are the global coordinate
charts of P5; frame changes are the Galilean transformations of P5, with
parameters and units as in [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. This
definition uses P5's frame class only. The transformation law of state
representatives under a change of inertial frame is a derived statement about
the model's operators and is established by the covariance theorems of this
page for translations and boosts; it is not an additional assumption of this
definition, and no Lorentz transformation law is claimed.

**(f) Status.** Clauses (a)-(e) record the readings of P1, P2, P5 and P6 in the
terminology of this page and fix the objects used by its theorems. They assert
no time evolution beyond what the autonomous-dynamics postulate P4 assigns
([[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]]
clause (iv)), no preparation or apparatus model, no detection model and no
empirical result. Massless particles, relativistic matter, radiation, singular
or unbounded potentials and boundary or confined realizations are separate
model assumptions with their own domains and self-adjointness statements; none
is obtained from this definition.

## Remarks

- **Why the class reading matters.** $H_{s}$ consists of almost-everywhere
  classes; the operators $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are defined on the classes of
  clause (b) and the core identities hold on the Schwartz classes. Phrases such
  as "the value of the wave function at $x$" are shorthand for a chosen
  representative and are not part of the model's state assignment.
- **Units.** The wave function, its momentum representative, the position and
  momentum spectral coordinates and the internal matrices are read in the
  units fixed by [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]; no numerical
  value, and in particular no value of $m$, $s$ or $\hbar$, is asserted beyond
  the exact defining constants of the current SI recorded there.

items.physical_scope: The kinematic reading of the massive-particle model postulate P5 for one particle of spin label s and mass parameter m>0: the component-valued state space L^2(R^3;C^(2s+1)) with its class reading and internal factor, the componentwise position and momentum operators with their declared units, the internal spin operators as matrix actions, the momentum-space representative, and the frame reading of the model. items.title: Position and momentum outcome laws of the massive spin-s model
items.statement:
Adopt the observable and probability postulate in the reading of
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]], the kinematics
and massive-particle model postulate P5, and the internal-factor assignment of
the postulate P6, all read for the spin-$s$ model of
[[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]] with mass parameter
$m>0$, spin label $s\in\{0,\tfrac12,1,\dots\}$ and $r=2s+1$
([[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]]), and assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H_{s}$ be the model's state space, $Q_{j},P_{k}$
its componentwise position and momentum operators, $U^{(s)}$ its momentum
transform, and let $\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_{A}(B)\psi\|^{2}$ be the outcome law
of an assigned sharp observable $A$ in a unit vector $\psi$
([[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (b)).
Then:

(a) for each $j$ the spectral projection-valued measure of $Q_{j}$ is
$$E_{Q_{j}}(B)=M_{\mathbf 1_{x_{j}^{-1}(B)}}\qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel}),$$
the componentwise multiplication by the indicator, and
$$\mu^{Q_{j}}_{\psi}(B)=\int_{x_{j}^{-1}(B)}\|\psi(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}^{2}\,dx;$$
the law is atomless, $\mu^{Q_{j}}_{\psi}(\{\lambda\})=0$ for every
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$, and $\sigma(Q_{j})=\mathbb R$;

(b) there is a unique regular projection-valued measure $G$ on the Borel sets
of $\mathbb R^{3}$ with
$$G(B_{1}\times B_{2}\times B_{3})=E_{Q_{1}}(B_{1})E_{Q_{2}}(B_{2})E_{Q_{3}}(B_{3})$$
for all Borel $B_{1},B_{2},B_{3}$, namely $G(B)=M_{\mathbf 1_{B}}$, and its
scalar law is the model's Born position law,
$$\mu^{G}_{\psi}(B)=\|G(B)\psi\|^{2}=\int_{B}\|\psi(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}^{2}\,dx;$$

(c) for each $k$ the spectral projection-valued measure of $P_{k}$ is
$$E_{P_{k}}(B)=U^{(s)-1}M_{\mathbf 1_{B}(p_{k})}U^{(s)},$$
and with $\psi_{p}:=U^{(s)}\psi$
$$\mu^{P_{k}}_{\psi}(B)=\int_{\{p\in\mathbb R^{3}:\,p_{k}\in B\}}\|\psi_{p}(p)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}^{2}\,dp;$$
the law is atomless and $\sigma(P_{k})=\mathbb R$;

(d) for every unitary $V\in U(r)$, with $V_{\times}$ the matrix action of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-ccr-and-internal-factor-commutation]] clause (b),
$$\mu^{Q_{j}}_{V_{\times}\psi}=\mu^{Q_{j}}_{\psi},\qquad \mu^{P_{k}}_{V_{\times}\psi}=\mu^{P_{k}}_{\psi};$$

(e) **Scope.** The statement is conditional on P2, P5 and P6 and the cited
mathematics, and extends the position and momentum laws of the massive model to
the spin-$s$ state space. No joint law of a position and a momentum observable
is asserted, no dynamics is used or claimed, and the identification of the
operators with concrete laboratory apparatus is a tested identification under
the preparation and apparatus postulate, not a consequence of this theorem;
no empirical result is recorded. Exact values have probability zero although
both spectra equal $\mathbb R$, so an exact value is an idealization outside
the sharp finite-resolution reading.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The postulates P2, P5, P6 read through [[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]]; the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice; the state space $H_{s}$ with $r=2s+1$; the operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$ and the unitaries $\Psi_{0},U^{(s)}$; a unit vector $\psi\in H_{s}$; Borel sets $B,B_{1},B_{2},B_{3}\subseteq\mathbb R$; a Borel set $B'\subseteq\mathbb R^{3}$; a unitary matrix $V\in U(r)$; a real $\lambda$.

[F1] **Outcome law.** For an assigned sharp observable $A$ with spectral PVM $E_{A}$ the law in a unit vector is $\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_{A}(B)\psi\|^{2}$, a probability measure on the Borel sets; the spectral support of $E_{A}$ is the spectrum $\sigma(A)$, and $\mu^{A}_{\psi}(\{\lambda\})=0$ unless $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ ([[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clauses (b)-(d)). Exact values of a quantity with no eigenvalues are idealizations outside the sharp assignment (clause (c) of the same definition, [[def-projection-valued-measure]]).

[F2] **Componentwise operators and their spectral measures.** $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are the componentwise operators of the model, self-adjoint with their maximal domains; $E_{Q_{j}}(B)=M_{\mathbf 1_{x_{j}^{-1}(B)}}$ and $E_{P_{k}}(B)=\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)*}M_{\mathbf 1_{\{2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}\in B\}}}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$ are their spectral PVMs ([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-ccr-and-internal-factor-commutation]] clauses (b),(c), [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clause (a)); the matrix action $V_{\times}$ commutes with these PVMs and is unitary for unitary $V$ ([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-ccr-and-internal-factor-commutation]] clauses (b)-(d)).

[F3] **Momentum representation.** $U^{(s)}=U^{(\cdot)}$ for $r=2s+1$ is unitary, $U^{(s)}D(P_{k})=D(M_{p_{k}})$ and $U^{(s)}P_{k}=M_{p_{k}}U^{(s)}$; on Schwartz classes the displayed integral formula holds and the Plancherel identity $\int\|U^{(s)}f\|^{2}dp=\int\|f\|^{2}dx$ ([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-momentum-representation]] clauses (a),(b)).

[F4] **Multiplication spectral measure.** For a $\sigma$-finite measure space and a real measurable finite-valued multiplier $m$, the multiplication operator $M_{m}$ is self-adjoint with regular spectral PVM $M_{\mathbf 1_{m^{-1}(B)}}$ and $\sigma(M_{m})$ equal to the essential range of $m$ ([[lem-nrqm-observables-l2-multiplication-spectral-measure]] clauses (a),(c),(d)); a regular PVM representing a self-adjoint operator is its spectral PVM ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]).

[F5] **Measure toolkit.** For $\sigma$-finite measure spaces, integrals of nonnegative product-measurable functions may be iterated ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); for nonnegative measurable $h$ the set function $A\mapsto\int_{A}h\,d\mu$ is a measure ([[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]); finite measures on the $\sigma$-algebra generated by a $\pi$-system that agree on the $\pi$-system and have equal mass are equal ([[lem-finite-measure-uniqueness-on-a-pi-system]]); the Euclidean Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R^{3}$ is generated by the rectangles ([[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]]). A coordinate hyperplane in $\mathbb R^{3}$ has Lebesgue measure zero: its indicator has iterated integral zero by [F5] because the inner integral over a singleton vanishes.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; read the spectral measures of the componentwise operators from the conjugation lemmas, compute the laws by Tonelli, construct the joint position projection-valued measure and prove its uniqueness on rectangles, and transport the momentum measure through the unitary momentum representation.

**Given:** The data of the statement and [F1]-[F5].

1.1 [Position spectral measure and law] [F2] gives $E_{Q_{j}}(B)=M_{\mathbf 1_{x_{j}^{-1}(B)}}$, so for a unit $\psi$, $\mu^{Q_{j}}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_{Q_{j}}(B)\psi\|^{2} =\int_{x_{j}^{-1}(B)}\|\psi(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}^{2}dx$ by [F1] and the definition of the componentwise norm. The measure is the indefinite integral $A\mapsto\int_{A}\|\psi\|^{2}dx$ of a nonnegative integrable function [F5], hence atomless: for every $\lambda$ the set $x_{j}^{-1}(\{\lambda\})$ is a coordinate hyperplane, whose indicator has iterated integral zero by [F5], so $\mu^{Q_{j}}_{\psi}(\{\lambda\})=0$. Finally the essential range of $x_{j}$ is $\mathbb R$ because every interval slab $x_{j}^{-1}((\lambda-\varepsilon,\lambda+\varepsilon))$ has positive Lebesgue measure, so [F4] gives $\sigma(Q_{j})=\mathbb R$. This proves (a). [F1, F2, F4, F5, algebra]

1.2 [Internal-factor invariance] Let $V\in U(r)$. By [F2] the matrix action $V_{\times}$ is unitary and commutes with $E_{Q_{j}}(B)$ and $E_{P_{k}}(B)$; hence $\mu^{Q_{j}}_{V_{\times}\psi}(B) =\|E_{Q_{j}}(B)V_{\times}\psi\|^{2} =\|V_{\times}E_{Q_{j}}(B)\psi\|^{2} =\|E_{Q_{j}}(B)\psi\|^{2}=\mu^{Q_{j}}_{\psi}(B)$, and the same computation with $P_{k}$ proves (d). [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 [Joint position law] Define $G(B):=M_{\mathbf 1_{B}}$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{3}$; each $G(B)$ is a bounded self-adjoint projection because pointwise multiplication by an indicator is one, and $G$ is a regular PVM: $G(B)G(C)=G(B\cap C)$, the total mass is $I$, and strong countable additivity follows by dominated convergence for $\|G(B)\psi-\sum_{n\le N}G(B_{n})\psi\|^{2} =\int\bigl|\mathbf 1_{B}-\sum_{n\le N}\mathbf 1_{B_{n}}\bigr|\,\|\psi\|^{2}$. On rectangles, $G(B_{1}\times B_{2}\times B_{3}) =M_{\mathbf 1_{B_{1}}(x_{1})\mathbf 1_{B_{2}}(x_{2})\mathbf 1_{B_{3}}(x_{3})} =E_{Q_{1}}(B_{1})E_{Q_{2}}(B_{2})E_{Q_{3}}(B_{3})$ by [F2], since the componentwise multipliers commute. For a unit $\psi$ the scalar law is $\mu^{G}_{\psi}(B)=\|G(B)\psi\|^{2}=\int_{B}\|\psi(x)\|^{2}dx$. If $G'$ is another regular PVM with the same rectangle values, then for every unit $\varphi$ the finite measures $B\mapsto\langle G(B)\varphi,\varphi\rangle$ and $B\mapsto\langle G'(B)\varphi,\varphi\rangle$ agree on the rectangles, a $\pi$-system generating the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R^{3}$ [F5], and have equal total mass $\|\varphi\|^{2}$; [F5] makes them equal on all Borel sets, and polarization recovers all pairings, so $G'=G$. This proves (b). [step 1.1, F2, F4, F5, algebra]

2.2 [Momentum spectral measure and law] By [F3] and [F4], $U^{(s)}$ is unitary, $D(M_{p_{k}})=U^{(s)}D(P_{k})$ and $M_{p_{k}}=U^{(s)}P_{k}U^{(s)-1}$; the multiplication operator $M_{p_{k}}$ on $L^{2}(dp;\mathbb C^{r})$ is self-adjoint with spectral PVM $M_{\mathbf 1_{\{p_{k}\in B\}}}$ [F4], so transporting through the unitary $U^{(s)}$ and using uniqueness of the spectral PVM [F4] gives $E_{P_{k}}(B)=U^{(s)-1}M_{\mathbf 1_{\{p_{k}\in B\}}}U^{(s)}$. For a unit $\psi$, $\mu^{P_{k}}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_{P_{k}}(B)\psi\|^{2} =\|M_{\mathbf 1_{\{p_{k}\in B\}}}U^{(s)}\psi\|^{2} =\int_{\{p_{k}\in B\}}\|\psi_{p}(p)\|^{2}dp$ [F3]. The law is the indefinite integral of the integrable function $\|\psi_{p}\|^{2}$ over a slice condition, hence atomless by the hyperplane argument of step 1.1; and the essential range of $p_{k}$ is $\mathbb R$, so $\sigma(P_{k})=\mathbb R$ [F4]. This proves (c). [step 1.1, F3, F4, algebra]

3.1 [Scope] Clauses (a)-(d) are consequences of P2, P5 and P6 as read by [[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]] together with the displayed mathematics; no dynamics, joint position-momentum statistics, apparatus model or empirical claim is used, and the last sentences of the statement record the scope. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 1.2] ∎

## Remarks

- **Relation to the spinless laws.** For $s=0$ one has $r=1$ and the statement
  reduces to the position and momentum outcome laws of the spinless massive
  model already established on the observables page; the present theorem
  supplies the component-valued case and the invariance of the spatial laws
  under the internal factor.
- **Nondegenerate continuum.** Both spectra equal $\mathbb R$ and both laws are
  atomless: the model admits no normalizable position or momentum eigenvector,
  and no exact value is an outcome with positive probability. Finite-resolution
  readings are the Borel bin probabilities displayed above.

B. Zwiebach, MIT 8.05 Quantum Physics II (Fall 2013), Chapter 1 'Wave Mechanics', Sections 4 and 6, printed pages 12-18 and 22-25 (PDF pages 12-18 and 22-25): the nature of the spectrum and the position and momentum representations
